evaluated.name: CashPerCapexDollar
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oancf, 3), MA(capx, 3)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The ratio of operating cash generated to capital spent measures how many dollars of internal cash each dollar of investment supports; high values identify self-funding, capital-light profit machines that are systematically undervalued relative to capital-hungry firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling profitability by investment outlay rather than by assets makes the signal a direct measure of investment discipline conditional on profitability, which no single-theme ratio captures. Three-year averaging removes lumpy capex cycles and one-off cash-flow spikes, and winsorization controls the exploding-denominator tail typical of ratio constructions.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitableShrinkerConditional
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(ib, at), 0.05), NEG(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms that clear a real profitability hurdle, shrinking or flat gross physical capacity signals management returning capital instead of chasing growth, and such firms are mispriced upward-drifting value plays; unprofitable firms' capacity cuts carry no such information.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator switches the investment-discipline signal on only for genuinely profitable firms, making the effect explicitly conditional rather than additive. Using gross PP&E growth rather than total asset growth focuses on deliberate capacity decisions rather than cash or working-capital noise.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginTrendVsCapexTrend
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose operating profitability is trending up while their reinvestment rate is trending down are quietly improving efficiency; the market underreacts because there is no visible expansion story, whereas rising capex intensity with flattening margins signals value-destroying growth.
evaluated.reasoning: This contrasts the direction of two multi-year states rather than their levels, capturing a divergence concept that neither theme expresses alone. Ranking both trends before differencing makes the scales comparable and keeps the spread robust to industry-level differences in capital intensity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DoubleCreditedGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors credit a firm twice when it is both highly profitable and rapidly expanding capacity, pushing prices above fundamentals; these doubly celebrated firms subsequently underperform as returns on new capacity mean-revert.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative form peaks only in the joint high-profitability, high-investment corner, which is precisely the overpricing quadrant of the economic story and cannot be produced by either theme in isolation. It provides the mirror-image test of the cash-cow hypothesis, so a reliably negative slope corroborates the mechanism from the short side.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SelfFundedVsExternallyFundedGrowth
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose profits comfortably cover their investment and that raise no outside capital are disciplined compounders, while firms funding expansion with new equity and debt are exploiting favorable sentiment about their profitability; the former outperform the latter.
evaluated.reasoning: Free cash flow after capex embeds profitability and investment jointly in the numerator, and subtracting the external-financing rank identifies who is paying for the investment, a discipline dimension absent from asset-growth measures. The construction separates internally financed restraint from externally financed empire building even when both groups show similar reported profitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: InternalCashPerCapexBroad
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MA(capx, 3)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms generating many dollars of internal cash earnings per dollar of capital expenditure are self-funding, capital-light profit machines whose returns are underpriced relative to capital-hungry peers with the same reported profitability.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the coverage failure of the winning CashPerCapexDollar signal by replacing the narrowly reported `oancf` with the much more widely available earnings-plus-depreciation cash proxy, keeping the same economic ratio of profit generation to investment outlay. Three-year averaging still smooths lumpy capex, and winsorization controls the small-denominator tail, so if the mechanism is real the FMB slope and alpha should survive at roughly triple the coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HarvestModeProfitability
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3), NEG(TREND(RATIO(capx, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms with persistently high operating profitability that are steadily *decelerating* their reinvestment rate have entered a harvest phase; because there is no growth narrative, the market underprices the cash they are about to return.
evaluated.reasoning: MarginTrendVsCapexTrend delivered the strongest alpha in the archive, but it is unclear whether the profitability trend or the capex downtrend drove it; pairing a stable profitability *level* with the capex-intensity downtrend isolates that design choice while remaining economically coherent. It also avoids the noisy 5-year margin trend, which should improve both coverage and portfolio stability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginVsInventoryBuild
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, sale)), RANK(GROWTH(invt, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: High-margin firms that are not building inventory are converting profitability into cash, whereas high-margin firms whose inventories swell are booking sales that have not yet been validated by demand and are therefore overpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves the investment leg from long-lived capital to working capital, an economically distinct discipline channel that also carries an information quality interpretation about the durability of reported margins. Rank differencing keeps the two legs on comparable scales and avoids the distress-contamination that ruined the PP&E-shrinkage construction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OrganicProfitVsInorganicExpansion
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), RANK(GROWTH(ADD(ppent, intan), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profitable firms that expand their combined tangible and intangible capital base rapidly, largely through acquisition and capitalized intangibles, are being credited twice for profitability and growth; profitable firms expanding that base slowly are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: DoubleCreditedGrowth failed because multiplication let profitability dominate; subtracting the investment rank instead makes the aggressive-expansion firms genuinely land in the short leg. Adding intangibles to net PP&E captures acquisition- and goodwill-driven empire building, which is where overpayment for growth is most likely, without relying on the sparsely reported `aqc` series.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitTimesLowReinvestment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(capx, ppent))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The mispricing is concentrated in the joint corner of high operating profitability and a low reinvestment rate relative to installed capacity: these are cash cows the market treats as ex-growth stories.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the correctly signed mirror of DoubleCreditedGrowth and tests whether a multiplicative interaction adds anything beyond an additive rank composite, since the product peaks only when both conditions hold simultaneously. Using capx scaled by net PP&E measures reinvestment intensity continuously rather than through capacity contraction, avoiding the distressed asset-sale firms that reversed the earlier conditional signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitPerHeadVsHiringGrowth
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(oiadp, emp), NEG(GROWTH(emp, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms earning high operating profit per employee while holding headcount flat are running lean, efficient operations whose cash generation is underappreciated; profitable firms hiring aggressively are investing in growth the market has already paid for.
evaluated.reasoning: Labor is an investment margin that management adjusts faster than physical capital, so it provides an independent read on investment discipline uncorrelated with capex-based measures. Scaling profit by employees rather than assets also sidesteps the shared `at` denominator, giving a genuinely real-side interaction between profitability intensity and expansion restraint.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashFlowPerCapexUnsmoothed
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, capx), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Operating cash flow per dollar of current capital expenditure identifies self-funding cash generators whose valuation does not reflect how little reinvestment their profits require.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best ratio signal used three-year averages on both legs and paid for it with 0.089 coverage; this strips the windows to isolate whether the alpha comes from the cash-flow-to-capex economics or from the smoothing, while roughly doubling usable observations. Because the profitability leg is cash-based rather than earnings-plus-depreciation, it should retain the FF5-orthogonal quality information that InternalCashPerCapexBroad lost.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: InvestmentProductivityTrend
evaluated.expression: TREND(WINSOR(RATIO(oiadp, capx), 1), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose operating profit per dollar of capital spending is rising over several years are becoming structurally more capital-efficient; the market extrapolates the level of profitability but not the improving productivity of investment.
evaluated.reasoning: This deliberately fuses the two structures that produced real FF5 alpha — a profit-per-investment ratio and a multi-year trend — into one variable, so it tests whether their success shares a single mechanism rather than being two accidents. Being a slope of a ratio, it is doubly removed from the linear profitability/investment directions spanned by RMW and CMA, which is where the earlier composites lost their alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginalReturnOnNewInvestment
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(oiadp, 1), LAG(capx, 1)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The incremental operating profit earned per dollar of the prior year's capital expenditure measures whether investment is actually creating value; firms with high marginal returns on new capital are underpriced, while firms whose profits stagnate after heavy spending are the overpriced growth-credited names.
evaluated.reasoning: All archive signals used average profitability against average investment; this is the first to test the *marginal* product of investment, a distinct economic mechanism that speaks directly to whether the market can distinguish productive from empire-building capex. The lagged denominator imposes a sensible investment-to-payoff timing structure and cannot be replicated by a static RMW/CMA blend.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryCapexRestraintVsProfit
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-profitable firms whose current reinvestment rate sits at the bottom of their *own* five-year history have chosen to harvest; because the restraint is relative to the firm's own norm rather than to the cross-section, it is not captured by the standard investment factor.
evaluated.reasoning: Cross-sectionally low investment is exactly what CMA prices, which is why earlier low-capex composites had their alpha absorbed; a within-firm position-in-history measure identifies a regime change in policy instead of a permanently capital-light business model. Pairing it with cash-based profitability keeps the interaction focused on firms that actually have profits to harvest.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitStabilityVsCapexVolatility
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), RANK(VOL(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Steady profitability combined with a smooth capital expansion path signals disciplined, well-governed capital allocation, whereas profitable firms with erratic lumpy expansion are chasing opportunities and destroying value; the market prices the profitability but not the allocation discipline.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces a second-moment investment channel, which is orthogonal to the level-based CMA exposure that flattened the earlier low-investment composites. It tests whether "investment discipline" is better measured by the stability of capital deployment than by its magnitude.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IndustryRelativeCapitalProductivity
evaluated.expression: IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 3), ppegt), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within an industry, firms that extract more operating profit from each dollar of installed gross capital are efficient asset-light operators whose future cash generation is underestimated relative to capital-heavy rivals with similar accounting profitability.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling profit by installed physical capital rather than by total assets makes the measure a true capital-productivity statistic, and industry z-scoring removes the mechanical capital-intensity differences that otherwise dominate this ratio. It tests the productivity-of-stock channel as a complement to the productivity-of-flow channel in Signals 1 and 3, which is a distinguishable economic hypothesis about efficiency rather than restraint.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryRestraintBroadProfit
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms with persistently high operating profitability whose current reinvestment rate sits low within their own five-year history are shifting from building to harvesting, and the market is slow to reprice this policy change.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one design choice in the archive's best signal: whether the 4.2% alpha requires cash-flow-based profitability or merely persistent operating profitability, while lifting coverage from 0.082 toward 0.11 by dropping `oancf`. If the alpha survives, the mechanism is the own-history investment leg rather than the cash-flow leg, which tells us where to concentrate the remaining generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashCowCapexOffPeak
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, TS_MAX(capx, 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-profitable firms whose capital spending has fallen far below its own five-year peak have completed an investment cycle and are about to convert capacity into free cash flow, a transition the market underprices.
evaluated.reasoning: Distance-from-own-peak is a sharper statement of the harvesting transition than a time-series percentile rank, because it measures how far spending has been cut in dollars rather than just its ordinal position. It keeps the within-firm conditioning that escaped CMA absorption while testing a different functional form of "investment discipline as a regime change."
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CumulativeReturnOnInvestmentCycle
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(oiadp, 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Three-year growth in operating profit per dollar of capital cumulatively invested over the same three years measures whether a full investment cycle actually paid off; firms with high realized payoffs are underpriced, and heavy spenders with no profit gain are the overpriced growth-credited names.
evaluated.reasoning: The one-year version of this idea produced a strong FF5 alpha but essentially no Fama-MacBeth slope, which points to timing mismatch and single-year noise rather than a false mechanism. Matching the profit change to the cumulative investment that produced it should convert tail-driven portfolio evidence into a coherent cross-sectional slope while retaining the payoff-realization economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitPerTotalInvestmentIncludingRD
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MA(oiadp, 3), ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Total investment includes intangible capital, so profit per dollar of combined physical and research investment better identifies genuinely capital-efficient cash generators than capex alone, which mislabels R&D-intensive firms as capital-light.
evaluated.reasoning: The profit-per-investment ratio family is the archive's most reliable, and its main measurement error is treating R&D-heavy firms as if they do not invest; treating unreported R&D as zero is the economically correct convention here rather than a coverage patch. This tests whether widening the investment base strengthens both the FMB slope and the alpha relative to the capex-only version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitGrowthOutpacingCapacityGrowth
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(GROWTH(oiadp, 1)), RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose operating profit is growing faster than their productive capacity are generating growth without capital, and this "growth for free" is underpriced relative to firms whose profit growth merely tracks the capacity they bought.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the failed level composites, both legs here are flows, so the signal is not a linear blend of the RMW profitability level and the CMA asset-growth level; it identifies the source of growth rather than its amount. It is also a much higher-coverage, shorter-horizon complement to the five-year trend divergence signal, which lets us see whether the divergence effect is slow-moving or immediate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DemeanedProfitInvestmentInteraction
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oibdp, at), 1)), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The mispricing is a genuine interaction: capacity expansion is most damaging for firms the market already celebrates for profitability, and profitability is most rewarding when unaccompanied by expansion; the cross-product of demeaned profitability and demeaned expansion isolates that quadrant structure.
evaluated.reasoning: Earlier rank products failed because ranks are non-negative and monotone, so their product remained a near-linear blend of the two factor directions; a product of z-scores is mean-zero in each leg and is therefore mechanically orthogonal to the linear RMW and CMA exposures that absorbed those signals. This is the cleanest available test of whether the interaction itself, rather than the two main effects, carries the abnormal return.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HarvestTransitionComposite
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), RATIO(capx, TS_MAX(capx, 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-profitable firms that are simultaneously spending at the low end of their own five-year reinvestment history and far below their own capex peak have unambiguously entered a harvesting phase, and this policy transition is repriced only slowly.
evaluated.reasoning: The two best archive signals used two different but individually noisy measures of own-history restraint (time-series percentile and distance from peak); combining them inside a single ranked restraint leg should cancel measurement noise and raise both ls_talpha and Sharpe rather than merely reshuffling the same firms. It keeps the cash-flow profitability leg that delivered the highest alpha and Sharpe in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HierarchicalProfitRestraint
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(COALESCE(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3))), RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The harvesting mechanism is the same whether profitability is measured in cash or in operating income; using cash flow when reported and operating profitability when not should preserve the cash-flow alpha while extending the signal to the pre-cash-flow-statement era and to non-reporters.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows a clean trade-off — oancf gives alpha 4.2% at coverage 0.082, oibdp gives 2.9% at 0.122 — and COALESCE is the economically correct way to prioritize the better measure without discarding firms. This directly tests whether the leading signal's alpha is coverage-limited or sample-specific, which matters for the remaining consolidation rounds.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FreeCashFlowOnInstalledCapital
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), ppent), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Free cash flow per dollar of installed productive capital measures how much surplus cash a firm's existing asset base throws off after funding its own investment needs; high values identify underpriced cash generators, low or negative values identify firms consuming cash to grow.
evaluated.reasoning: This keeps the profit-per-investment ratio structure that reliably produced alpha but changes the economics from "how cheaply do they grow" to "how much surplus does the installed base yield," netting investment out of the numerator rather than dividing by it. Scaling by net PP&E rather than the lumpy capex flow should also stabilize portfolio composition, addressing the modest ls_talpha of the unsmoothed oancf/capx version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitAccelVsCapexDecel
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(ACCEL(RATIO(oiadp, at))), RANK(ACCEL(RATIO(capx, ppent))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The turning point matters more than the trend: firms whose profitability is accelerating just as their reinvestment rate decelerates are at the inflection from investment phase to cash harvest, and the market anchors on the prior phase.
evaluated.reasoning: Trend divergence over five years produced the archive's most precise alpha (t 3.71), so the natural next question is whether the information is in the level of the slopes or in their change, a distinguishable timing hypothesis rather than a cosmetic variant. Second differences are also mechanically orthogonal to the level-based RMW and CMA exposures that flattened the static composites.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MaintenanceCapexCashCow
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(WINSOR(MA(RATIO(capx, dp), 3), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital expenditure relative to depreciation measures investment against the firm's own replacement requirement; cash-profitable firms spending near or below maintenance levels are deliberately liquidating capacity into cash and are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: Normalizing capex by depreciation is a firm-specific benchmark like the own-history measures that escaped CMA absorption, rather than a cross-sectional capital-intensity ranking, and it has a sharp economic threshold at one. Earlier evidence that (ib+dp)/capx lost its alpha suggests the depreciation channel needs to sit in the *investment* leg with genuine cash profitability on the other side, which is exactly the structure tested here.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitableIntangibleTilt
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3), WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among profitable firms, investment tilted toward research rather than physical capacity is systematically underpriced because intangible investment is expensed rather than capitalized, so reported profitability understates the true earning power of these firms.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign reversal of ProfitPerTotalInvestmentIncludingRD (−3.9%, t −3.24) revealed that R&D-heavy profitable firms sit in the outperforming leg, so investment *composition* is a distinct and oppositely signed channel from investment *restraint*. Treating unreported R&D as zero is the standard convention, and this proposal turns an accidental reversal into an explicit, testable mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HarvestAndIntangibleTilt
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(COALESCE(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), SUMRANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Underpriced cash generators are profitable firms that both hold physical reinvestment below their own historical norm and direct the spending they do undertake toward research rather than capacity; the two forms of investment discipline are complementary and should compound.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's two strongest signals isolate different investment legs — own-history restraint (Sharpe 0.46–0.56) and research tilt (fmb 4.18) — while sharing the same profitability channel, so merging them tests additivity rather than restating either. The COALESCE profitability hierarchy is retained because it demonstrably raised alpha, t-stat, and coverage simultaneously in generation 4.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ResearchStockVsPhysicalStock
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3), WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 5), ppegt), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for mismeasured earning power is the accumulated stock of research capital relative to installed physical capital, not the single-year spending mix; profitable firms whose economic capital is mostly unbooked research are the most underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: ProfitableIntangibleTilt used a one-year flow share and delivered a strong FMB slope but a modest Sharpe, consistent with a noisy annual mix measure; cumulating five years of R&D into a stock and benchmarking it against gross PP&E should stabilize portfolio composition. This isolates the flow-versus-stock design choice inside the composition channel rather than duplicating it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashProfitTrendVsCapexTrend
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(TREND(COALESCE(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(oibdp, at)), 5)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose cash profitability is trending up while their reinvestment rate trends down are transitioning to harvest, and cash-based profitability tracks that transition more faithfully than accrual operating income.
evaluated.reasoning: MarginTrendVsCapexTrend still holds the archive's most precise alpha (3.6%, t 3.71) using accrual operating profitability, while the cash-flow hierarchy lifted every statistic in the restraint family; this applies that one proven substitution to the trend family. It is a deliberate single-design-choice test whose outcome tells us whether the cash-flow advantage is general or specific to level-based restraint measures.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IndustryRelativeRestraintCashCow
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(COALESCE(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3))), RANK(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment norms are set by technology within an industry, so a profitable firm spending well below its industry's reinvestment norm is exercising genuine discipline, whereas a low absolute capex rate may merely reflect an asset-light industry.
evaluated.reasoning: Own-history conditioning succeeded because it escaped the cross-sectional low-investment direction that CMA already prices; industry-relative conditioning is the other natural way to strip out permanent capital-intensity differences, and it applies to firms without long histories. Comparing it head-to-head with the TS_RANK version identifies which benchmark carries the harvesting information.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsQualityAndCapexRestraint
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))), RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose earnings are fully backed by cash and that are simultaneously restraining reinvestment relative to their own history are true cash generators; firms with accrual-inflated earnings that keep spending are the ones the market credits for both quality and growth it will not receive.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the profitability *level* leg with an earnings *quality* leg, a distinct economic dimension that explains why cash-flow profitability outperformed accrual profitability throughout the archive rather than just exploiting it. Because the accrual gap is nearly orthogonal to the RMW profitability level, the interaction should not be absorbed by FF5 in the way the earlier level composites were.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RealizedPayoffPlusProfitability
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(oiadp, 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that are both persistently profitable and can show that their last three years of capital spending actually produced incremental operating profit have demonstrated value-creating investment, whereas persistent profitability with no payoff on cumulative spending signals capital destruction.
evaluated.reasoning: The cumulative-payoff ratio produced a reliable FF5 alpha (2.8%, t 2.97) but almost no Fama-MacBeth slope (1.24), the signature of a tail-driven measure; anchoring it with a smooth profitability level should supply the missing cross-sectional monotonicity while preserving the payoff-realization economics. This repairs the specific failure mode of that channel instead of discarding it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FourChannelHarvestScore
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(COALESCE(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))), SUMRANK(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0))), NEG(TREND(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Harvesting is a multi-dimensional state: high cash profitability, reinvestment low relative to the firm's own history, a research-tilted spending mix, and a multi-year downward path in reinvestment intensity each carry independent information about underpriced cash generators.
evaluated.reasoning: The three-channel version delivered the archive's best alpha (5.3%, t 4.98) and the capex-trend leg independently powered a 5.0% alpha in the trend family, so adding it as a fourth equally weighted channel is the direct test of whether additivity continues or saturates. Because the level and slope of reinvestment are distinct states, this is not a restatement of the restraint leg already present.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: QualityAugmentedHarvest
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(SUMRANK(COALESCE(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-backed earnings are the credible form of profitability, so adding an accrual-gap quality screen to the harvest score should concentrate the long leg in firms whose reported profits are real and whose investment discipline is deliberate rather than a symptom of hidden weakness.
evaluated.reasoning: EarningsQualityAndCapexRestraint produced a 4.9% alpha with only two channels and coverage 0.082, showing the accrual gap carries information beyond the profitability level itself. This asks whether the quality dimension adds to the flagship or merely re-expresses the cash-flow hierarchy already embedded in it, which is the key remaining ambiguity in the winning family.
